topic: Moser's Circle Problem: The Mystery of Dividing the Plane
target_audience: High school students with an interest in combinatorics and pattern recognition

outline.topic: Moser's Circle Problem: The Mystery of Dividing the Plane
outline.target_audience: High school students with an interest in combinatorics and pattern recognition

sections.title: The Hook: How many pieces?
sections.content: Introduce the problem: Place n points on the circumference of a circle and connect every pair of points with a chord. What is the maximum number of regions created inside the circle? Start with simple cases (n=1, 2, 3) to show how the circle is segmented.
sections.example: Visualize a pizza with 3 toppings on the edge. Connecting them creates 4 slices.

sections.title: Pattern Recognition (The Trap)
sections.content: Calculate regions for n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Show the values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Ask students to predict the next number. Most will naturally guess 32 (powers of 2). Explain that this is a classic mathematical 'trap' where early patterns don't always hold.
sections.example: A series of animations showing 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 regions appearing as points are added.

sections.title: The Geometric Insight
sections.content: Briefly explain the prerequisite: Euler’s Formula for planar graphs (V - E + F = 2). Shift focus to counting vertices (V) and edges (E) formed by the intersections of chords. Crucially, show that every intersection of two chords creates a new region.
sections.example: An animation showing a 6th point being added, creating 31 regions instead of the expected 32, highlighting the 'missing' piece.

sections.title: The General Formula
sections.content: Present the binomial coefficient formula: R = (n choose 4) + (n choose 2) + 1. Explain that each term corresponds to the geometry: (n choose 4) accounts for the interior intersection points, and (n choose 2) accounts for the chords.
sections.example: A visual 'building block' diagram where we assemble the formula from the shapes created by points and intersections.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of Skepticism
sections.content: Summarize the lesson: Patterns are useful, but rigorous proof is necessary. Remind students that Moser's problem is a testament to why mathematicians never trust a sequence until they understand the underlying structure.
sections.example: A 'detective' character closing a case file titled 'The Pattern that Lied,' showing the shift from 32 to 31.

lecture_lines: Place n points on a circle.

storyboard.title: Pattern Recognition (The Trap)

Show a question mark #FF0000 next to 32 to prompt the viewer.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Insight
lecture_lines: Use Euler's Formula: V - E + F = 2.

Animate counting vertices V (points) and edges E (chord segments) #00FFFF.
Color one new region #FF00FF as lines intersect.
Cross out the power of 2 pattern #FF0000.

storyboard.title: The General Formula
lecture_lines: The formula is R = (n choose 4) + (n choose 2) + 1.
animations: Write the formula R = (n choose 4) + (n choose 2) + 1 in #FFFFFF.
Highlight (n choose 4) in #00FFFF representing interior intersection points.
Highlight (n choose 2) in #FFD700 representing the chords drawn.
